title: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)
word: the crow and the first verse
hook: Brahma visits the troubled poet and tells him the verse was meant
carry: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)

segments.voice: Yesterday: krauncha, and the hunter's arrow. Valmiki's grief, shoka, poured out as verse, shloka.

Valmiki goes back to his hermitage, but he can't let it go. He bathes, he sits, and the verse keeps playing in his head, along with the guilt of having cursed someone. You know the feeling: a sentence you said today, replaying at night. Then a visitor arrives. Not a wandering sage this time. Brahma himself, the creator, four-faced, the one the whole world comes from. And Valmiki, still lost in the bird's grief, can't stop saying the verse, even in front of him.
screen: `REPLAYING IT AT NIGHT.` → `A VISITOR: BRAHMA.` → `STILL SAYING THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Brahma smiles and settles it. Don't be troubled, he says. That verse came from me; it was meant to. Now tell the whole story of Rama, as Narada told it to you, in this same meter. What's hidden will be shown to you: what Rama did and said, what Sita did, what happened in private and in public. Not one word you speak in this poem will be false. Then the promise people still quote: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow on the earth, so long will the story of Rama be told. Brahma disappears, and Valmiki's students repeat the verse to each other in wonder. Valmiki sits facing east on a seat of sacred grass, sips water, and turns inward. The story comes to him, the book says, in vision, all of it, laughter, talk, walks, as clearly as if it were in front of him. He composes it. The tradition gives the count: twenty-four thousand verses, in what we now know as seven books. Then he needs someone to carry it. Two boys live in his hermitage, twins with beautiful voices, Kusha and Lava. He teaches them the whole poem by heart, and they sing it at gatherings of sages and later in a king's court. Here's the turn: the twins are Rama's own sons, though Rama doesn't know them yet. The story will be sung to its own hero.
screen: `THE VERSE CAME FROM ME, SAYS BRAHMA.` · `NO WORD OF IT WILL BE FALSE.` · `AS LONG AS MOUNTAINS AND RIVERS.` · `TWO BOYS SING IT BY HEART.` · then, large: `TWENTY-FOUR THOUSAND VERSES.`

segments.voice: Sit like Valmiki on his grass seat and take four slow breaths, counting them like the four quarters of a verse, then let the counting go. If a sentence from today keeps replaying, let it play once more, then set it down beside you.
The crow and the first verse. Brahma tells Valmiki the verse was meant, and gives him the whole story of Rama to tell in that same meter.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE FIRST VERSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the crow and the first verse, the origin of poetry. As long as mountains stand, the story goes on. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Ramayana has long been passed on by heart and in song, and many Hindus recite or listen to its verses at home and in temples; the tradition of reciters traces itself back to Kusha and Lava singing Valmiki's poem.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 2–4 frame the epic: Brahma's commission, Valmiki's vision, and Kusha and Lava as its first reciters, kushilava, the old word for wandering bards.

chat.says: Who were the very first people to sing the Ramayana?
options: Twin boys, Kusha and Lava, who learned it by heart. They were Rama's own sons.
Valmiki's students at the river, who sang it to the hunter as an apology.
Brahma's attendants, who sang it in heaven before it reached the earth.
chat.meaning: Valmiki taught the poem to twins Kusha and Lava, who sang it for sages and in a king's court. They are Rama's sons, though he doesn't know it yet.

Kusha.meaning: one of the twin singers, Rama's son

Lava.meaning: the other twin singer, Rama's son

notes: Brahma's promise (mountains and rivers) paraphrased from Bala Kanda 2; confirm.
Bala Kanda 4 gives 24,000 shlokas and speaks of six kandas plus the Uttara; the script says 'what we now know as seven books'. Confirm framing.
Kushilava as a word for bards and its link to Kusha and Lava is a traditional association; scholars debate the direction of the etymology. Confirm or drop from the trapdoor.
The 'four breaths like four quarters' practice is the script's own.
